Inheritance of Genes
Dr Dan Corbett

pages.title: Slide 2
pages.text:
Why is this Important?
• Our genetic material is the blueprint which tells our cells what to do, and
  how to do it
• So, our cells need to contain this blueprint so that they can function
  correctly
• Your cells replace themselves at a rate of about 300 billion cells PER
  DAY – that’s four million a SECOND
• They’re constantly being replaced with exact copies of the previous ones
  – this is key to survival
• It’s important for us to know how this works, for lots of reasons
• All of this also relates to how our genetic material is passed on to our
  offspring (our children) – this is where they get their blueprints from
• Understanding these processes is the key to understanding how we can
  treat genetic conditions, as we’ll be able to more easily identify targets!

Inheritance of Genes

Part 1. DNA Replication

media.webLabel: Open slide 3 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 4
pages.text:
DNA Replication – An Overview
• We’ll consider different parts of the cell cycle over these next three
  lectures
• DNA replication is a key part of this cycle
• It makes sure that the newly-divided “daughter” cells contain a copy
  of DNA from their “parent” cell
• Once the DNA in a cell has been copied, the cell can then divide,
  giving us new daughter cells each of which will have the same
  blueprint as the parent cell

The overall aim: produce two copies of our DNA from the one that
                     we have to begin with!

media.webLabel: Open slide 4 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 5
pages.text:
DNA Replication – Duplicating Strands
• A key thing to remember is that both strands in the DNA starting point are used as
  templates for replication
• Complementary base pairing allows for two exact copies of double-stranded DNA to be
  produced
• Because of this, we say that DNA replication is semi-conservative - each new cell ends
  up with one strand of the original DNA – the other strand is freshly synthesised!

practice.title: Tracing the old strands
practice.prompt: A student draws two product DNA molecules after a single round of replication. Both parental strands sit in one molecule and both new strands sit in the other. How would you redraw the product molecules using the lecture’s model?
practice.answer: Give each double helix one parental strand and one newly made complementary strand. That distribution is what semi-conservative means.

pages.title: Slide 6
pages.text:
The Tools for the Job
• Unsurprisingly, DNA replication is pretty complicated
• Because of this, we need a few tools to make this happen –
  they’ll do their job at different parts of the process:
    • The DNA!
    • DNA helicase unwinds the DNA double helix
    • Single-strand binding proteins keep the single-stranded
      DNA stable, preventing the helix reforming prematurely
    • DNA primase makes short RNA primers to initiate replication
    • DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the growing DNA
      chains
    • RNase removes RNA primers
    • DNA ligase stitches gaps between DNA fragments together

media.webLabel: Open slide 6 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 7
pages.text:
DNA Replication – The Process
1. DNA helicase binds at an origin of replication– it then unwinds the
   strands, exposing the single strands of DNA nucleotides
2. Single-strand binding proteins bind to each of the strands, keeping
   them stable and separate
3. DNA primase recognises bits of the exposed DNA strands and drops an
   RNA primer at that portion – this is the starting point for the addition of
   nucleotides to the chain
4. DNA polymerase binds to the primer and works along the DNA chain,
   bringing nucleotides over to it, extending the new chain which started
   with the primer – these nucleotides are matched up by complementary
   base pairing
5. Depending on the chain being read, a continuous or discontinuous
   chain of DNA nucleotides is made – more on that in a few minutes!

media.webLabel: Open slide 7 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 8
pages.text:
DNA Replication – The Process

7. This process continues, with nucleotides being added, extending the new
   DNA strand in the 5’ to 3’ direction – DNA polymerase can only add
   nucleotides to the 3’ end of the growing chain
8. Eventually, there is no more DNA to replicate – we’ve reached the end of
   the chromosome, or two replication bubbles meet – this ends the
   process
9. Once this has all been done, the new strands are bound to their
   complementary strands with hydrogen bonds, and stabilised
10. The result – two new DNA molecules, each of which contain one strand
    from the original double strand, and a new strand which has just been
    manufactured!

pages.title: Slide 10
pages.text:
DNA Replication – Leading and
Lagging Strands
• Earlier, we said that the new DNA chain was synthesised in the 5’ to 3’ direction...
• ...and that DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3’ end of the new chain
• But as we also know, DNA strands come together in an antiparallel way
• So, how does this work when it comes to DNA synthesis?
• Depending on the chain that it is synthesising, DNA polymerase will work towards the
  replication fork or away from the replication fork
• If it’s working towards the replication fork, it can easily add on a new nucleotide to the
  new DNA chain in the 5’ to 3’ direction – the addition of nucleotides follows behind the
  replication fork as it opens up
• But, if it’s working away from the replication fork, this causes a problem - DNA
  polymerase can’t add nucleotides to the 5′ end of the growing chain, so it’ll have to
  regularly stop and wait for more of the double helix to unwind
• So, this time, DNA polymerase will make smaller chain fragments of DNA in the 5’ to 3’
  direction – called Okazaki fragments – and then join them together!

pages.title: Slide 11
pages.text: Still from the leading and lagging strand animation. It shows two lines representing the DNA double helix. The preceding slide explains continuous synthesis of the leading strand and the short fragments of the lagging strand.

media.webLabel: Open slide 11 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 12
pages.jumpLabel: • Lagging strands give us two more things to do:
pages.text:
• Lagging strands give us two more things to do:

   1. Remove the RNA primers from each fragment and replace them with
      DNA nucleotides – RNAase helps with that
   2. Join the fragments together (ligate them) – DNA ligase helps with that!

media.webLabel: Open slide 12 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 13
pages.text:
…and that’s it!
• This process will continue along multiple replication bubbles
  until the entire length of the DNA has been replicated
• At that point, we’ve ended up with two daughter chromatids –
  the copies of the chromosome
• These are now ready to enter into a new cell…
• …as the current one that they’re in starts to divide!
• This is what allows the new cells to inherit DNA and genes
  from the “parent” cell!

  With that all in mind, let’s start to think about how those
cells divide to allow us to grow sustain ourselves – MITOSIS!

pages.text:
Inheritance of Genes

Part 2. Mitosis – Producing Identical
Cells

media.webLabel: Open slide 14 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 15
pages.jumpLabel: Mitosis – A Key Part of the Cell Cycle!
pages.text:
Mitosis – A Key Part of the Cell Cycle!
• Mitosis is key to our survival – it produces new cells for growth -
  it’s what allowed us to become more than a single cell!
• It’s also there to replace damaged or dead cells, helping with
  things like wound healing and tissue regeneration
• Mitosis ensures that the newly-produced daughter cells receive
  an exact copy of the parent cell’s DNA, maintaining the number
  of chromosomes and ensuring normal function – this is still
  inheritance, just not as we might have thought of it before!
• Once all of this is done, we end up with cells which are in a
  position to grow and function in the way that we need, including
  carrying out all of the other steps of the cell cycle!

pages.title: Slide 17
pages.text:
Stages of Mitosis – Prophase
• DNA, initially stretched out a bit as chromatin,
  condenses into visible chromosomes
• We’ll see the sister chromatids here – each of
  the pairs of identical chromosomes are joined at
  a centromere
• The nuclear envelope starts to break down,
  making the DNA accessible to the rest of the cell
• Microtubules begin to assemble into the mitotic
  spindle
• Centrosomes (which organise the mictrotubules    One
  which are involved) move to opposite poles of chromatid
  the cell, helping those spindles to form

media.webLabel: Open slide 17 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 18
pages.text:
Stages of Mitosis – Prometaphase

• This is a stage that we haven’t mentioned yet, which
  happens between prophase and metaphase!
• The nuclear envelope breaks down fully
• Those microtubule spindles attach to the chromosomes at
  the centromere
• The microtubules then begin to apply a pulling force to the chromosomes,
  pulling them back and forth to get them to line up
• This sets the stage for a key checkpoint later in the process — the cell ensures
  all chromosomes are attached correctly to spindle fibres before moving into
  anaphase
• If everything is good, we can move on to the next stage!

media.webLabel: Open slide 18 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 19
pages.text:
Stages of Mitosis – Metaphase


• All of the chromosomes are fully aligned on the
  equator of the cell – giving us the metaphase
  plate
• The centromere is more firmly attached to the
  microtubule spindles
• Everything is now ready to go and the chromatids
  can be separated – on to anaphase!

media.webLabel: Open slide 19 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 20
pages.text:
Stages of Mitosis – Anaphase

• The proteins holding the sister chromatids together are
  cleaved, allowing the chromatids to separate
• Each chromatid, now an individual chromosome, is rapidly
  pulled toward the side of the cell where it is attached by the
  microtubule spindle…
• …this happens due to the microtubules shortening!
• Other microtubules which are involved start to push the
  sides of the cell apart, getting the cell splitting process
  underway

media.webLabel: Open slide 20 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 21
pages.text:
Stages of Mitosis – Telophase

• The chromosomes start to relax a little, going back to
  their resting state
• New nuclear envelopes start to form from those
  fragments we created earlier!
• The mitotic spindles break down, and the microtubules
  they’re made from are broken up into their parts
• We’ll say that mitosis is complete when the two
  separate nuclei are fully formed!
• We can now start working on splitting the cell into its
  two daughters - cytokinesis

media.webLabel: Open slide 21 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 22
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Two nuclei in one cell
pages.text:
Cytokinesis
• We’re now out of mitosis, but we don’t have two cells which
  share our DNA - yet!
• During cytokinesis, we’ll see the parent cell's cytoplasm
  dividing to provide each daughter cell with its own
  environment and organelles
• A ring of actin filaments forms at the centre of the cell,
  pulling the membrane tight and leading to the separation of
  the two cells
• Two genetically identical daughter cells are formed, each
  with its own set of organelles, nucleus, and cell membrane!
• These daughter cells then enter into the G1 phase, getting
  ready to divide later and starting things all over again!

media.webLabel: Open slide 22 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Two nuclei in one cell
practice.prompt: An image shows a cell with two daughter nuclei. The cytoplasm has yet to separate into two compartments. Which process completes physical separation of the daughter cells? What visible change would support your answer?
practice.answer: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm. In the animal-cell example the membrane constricts until there are two separate daughter cells.

pages.title: Slide 23
pages.text: A microscopy still shows a cell with a bright central region. This visual follows the description of cytokinesis on slide 22. The PDF contains one still frame.

media.webLabel: Open slide 23 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 24
pages.text:
…and that’s that!
• After all of that, we now have two cells which are genetically
  identical to the cell that we started with
• They each have their own nucleus, which contains a full set of
  chromosomes, and all of the organelles, other machinery, and
  materials which they need to survive and grow
• All of this allows us to grow and repair tissues, and replace
  dead cells too!
• But what if we don’t want to replicate cells fully, and instead, we
  want to make cells which we can combine with a partner’s cells
  to make a new version of ourselves?
• We’ll need MEIOSIS to do this!

media.webLabel: Open slide 24 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 25
pages.text:
Inheritance of Genes

Part 3. Meiosis – Splitting Genetic
Content

media.webLabel: Open slide 25 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 26
pages.text:
Why Meiosis?
• Meiosis is an incredibly important part of our reproduction
• It involves the production of sex cells, which are very different from our
  somatic cells
• We can also refer to sex cells as gametes, and can classify them even
  further:
    • The male gamete is the sperm cell
    • The female gamete is the egg or ova cell
• One of the most key aspects of these cells is that they contain half the
  amount of DNA that our somatic cells contain
   • Somatic cells = 46 chromosomes (23 pairs – one set from our mother,
     the other from our father) – also known as diploid
   • Sex cells = 23 chromosomes – also known as haploid
• This factor is what leads to the genetic variation of our offspring – the
  chromosomes of our parents mix to give us a full set of genes!

media.webLabel: Open slide 26 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 27
pages.text:
How does it Work?                                            (2n)




• Meiosis involves the same four general
  stages that we saw in mitosis
• But – there are two more major stages
  with cell division happening at the end
  of both of them
• Importantly, we DON’T see genetic         n (duplicated)
  replication happening between
  meiosis I and II
• This means that the second time the
  cells separate, we end up with cells
  which contain HALF the amount of
  DNA

media.webLabel: Open slide 27 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 28
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · A one-set cell with paired copies
pages.text:
How does it Work?
• During meiosis I, we’ll see homologous chromosomes pairing up
• So, rather than seeing the sister chromatids in the chromosome separate…
• …the sister chromatids stay connected, and are separated out into one of two
  cells
• This means that the cells produced here contain 23 chromosomes (haploid),
  duplicated as sister chromatids!
• When we get into meiosis II, we’ll then see those sister chromatids being
  separated – but remember, there hasn’t been a DNA replication step before
  Meiosis II!
• So in meiosis II, we see two cells with 23 sister chromatids being separated out
  into two more cells with 23 single chromatids – half of a full set!
• We end up with four new cells in total, each containing half a full set of DNA

media.webLabel: Open slide 28 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: A one-set cell with paired copies
practice.prompt: In a meiotic drawing a daughter cell has one chromosome from each homologous pair, but its chromosomes still have two sister chromatids each. Which division has just occurred, and what will separate next?
practice.answer: Meiosis I has separated the homologues. The cell is already haploid even though its chromosomes are duplicated. In meiosis II, sister chromatids separate.

pages.title: Slide 30
pages.text:
Meiosis – A Source of Genetic
Variation
• Because of the way meiosis works, it can bring about a
  lot of genetic variation
• The first way that this can happen is by the crossing
  over of the content of those homologous
  chromosomes…
• …and the other is by the independent assortment of
  the homologous pairs during meiosis I

media.webLabel: Open slide 30 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Two explanations for variation
practice.prompt: In one drawing paired chromosomes exchange segments. In another, intact homologous pairs can line up in different orientations before separating. Which mechanism produces variation in each drawing? State the visible clue.
practice.answer: Exchange of segments identifies crossing over. Variation in how whole pairs align identifies independent assortment. The lecture distinguishes both mechanisms, then illustrates them on pages 31 and 32.

pages.title: Slide 31
pages.text:
Meiosis – Crossing Over
    • After replication of the DNA and entry into prophase I, chromosomes will
      condense as in mitosis, but in addition, homologous chromosomes will pair up
    • As they do so, they’ll interact with one another, exchanging material
    • This means that we’ll see crossing over of genetic material between the
      maternal and paternal chromosomes that we’ve got in our cells

pages.title: Slide 32
pages.text:
Meiosis – Random Independent
Assortment


• As meiosis I occurs, homologous pairs line up and are
  separated out into one of two cells
• The way each pair lines up is random – each one could be on
  one side, or the other
• This means that the homologous pairs can separate out in
  multiple combinations!

media.webLabel: Open slide 32 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.text:

pages.title: Slide 34
pages.jumpLabel: Meiosis – Bringing it all Back Together!
pages.text:
Meiosis – Bringing it all Back Together!
• After all of this, we have our
  sex cells, each of which
  contain 23 chromosomes –
  they are haploid
• We need our body cells to be
  diploid and contain 23 PAIRS
  of chromosomes – 46 in total
• This will happen via the
  process of fertilisation!
• Once this happens, our somatic
  cells start to replicate, and
  grow, growing us – and we’re
  back to mitosis all over again!

media.webLabel: Open slide 34 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 35
pages.text:
To Sum Up…
• We’ve now gone from thinking about the basics of how DNA
  replicates, turning one DNA molecule into two…
• …and thought about how this creates the DNA that we need to allow
  our cells to split in various ways
• One of these ways gives us two cells which are exactly the same -
  MITOSIS …
• …and the other gives us four cells which contain half of the DNA
  we need to function - MEIOSIS
• In that latter case, doing what we need to to put those two halves
  together gives us a new combination of DNA, which in turn
  generates a new organism with some of its own traits!

media.webLabel: Open slide 35 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 36
pages.text:
Next Time…

• We’ll think a bit about the fact that cell replication
  doesn’t just go on uncontrolled…
• …at least, it shouldn’t when we’re healthy!
• There is a significant amount of control of these
  processes going on, which will help our cells to know
  when to replicate, and importantly, when not to replicate
• This fine balance is the basis of our health…
• …and if that balance is upset, the basis of cancer!
